nodes.label: The separate signatory table was removed
nodes.source_location: Where this stands — read this first when resuming
nodes.rationale: The design assumed a signatory is a person with a typed name and typed position title kept in its own table. Once real fuel documents were typed out on 27 August 2026, nobody's title turned out to be typed: it is a caption printed on the form, or read from the person's own record. Nothing had been built, so the correction cost an edit.

nodes.label: Signature block
nodes.source_location: Vocabulary / The design as it now stands
nodes.rationale: The whole printed block where somebody signs: its label, the name, and the title underneath. Each block carries two rules written in the code — who may be chosen (any employee, a named unit's staff, anyone able to do something, one particular post, or nobody) and where the printed title comes from (a caption on the form, or the person's own title as it was at the time).

nodes.label: Caption
nodes.source_location: Vocabulary / Caption lines need nothing stored but a person
nodes.rationale: A title printed on the paper itself, such as "Driver", "Section Incharge" or "GSU Representative": the same words appear no matter who is named, so the system stores nothing and anybody may be chosen. The test is where the words come from, not what they look like. "Designation" is deliberately not used for this, since in this project a designation means a role on a group.

nodes.label: A document stores a reference to an employee history row
nodes.rationale: Storing the name as text freezes a typing mistake permanently across every record that used it, and nobody would remember which thirty records those were. A reference lets a misspelling be corrected everywhere at once while a marriage or promotion opens a new version and leaves old documents alone. One column per signature block, which may be blank.

nodes.label: Config table (fuel.gsu_org_unit, fuel.penr_officer)
nodes.source_location: How a signature block knows who may be chosen
nodes.rationale: One row per setting, a fixed key in code and a plain text value the office fills in, so no row id is hardcoded. Protection is a check before deleting or deactivating an org unit rather than a foreign key, because a foreign key would only have caught deletion and deactivation is an ordinary column change. Rejected alternatives: a fixed code column on org_unit, typed columns on the config table, and deriving the unit from whoever first opens the GSU page. Not built yet — it waits for the fuel work.

nodes.label: Signatory list built from the document's filed date
nodes.source_location: The list is built from the document's filed date, not from today
nodes.rationale: The form asks who was valid on the paper's own date, comparing valid_from and valid_until, rather than who is working today. A slip filed last month still offers the people valid then so it can be reprinted and signed per procurationem; a slip filed today does not; and editing an old document needs no special case. This is why separation must close the open history row and not only change a status.

nodes.label: Signing happens on paper only
nodes.rationale: The system prepares and prints documents with the right names; the paper is then carried around and signed by hand. An earlier answer saying signing happened both on paper and in the system created a problem that no longer exists, because signers with no account could never approve inside the system. A block may legitimately be printed blank.

nodes.label: Signature blocks are fixed in the code, one column each
nodes.rationale: Letting an admin add or rename blocks from a screen would let them break the fixed layout of the printed page. Each document gets one column per block, so the line is the column name and no label is stored. Adding or renaming a block is a developer change, accepted deliberately. Applies per document rather than per report, since the fuel report is three documents printed together.

nodes.label: The three fuel documents (Withdrawal Slip, Trip Ticket, RIS)
nodes.source_location: Appendix — real signing blocks from the fuel documents
nodes.rationale: Typed out by the user from physical paper on 26 August 2026 and used as evidence rather than as a decision. Nine signature blocks in total; the same names came out spelled differently on two passes (Olaivar/Olivar, Gonzaga/Gongaza), which is a live example of why a misspelling must be correctable everywhere at once.

nodes.label: OIC (Officer-in-Charge), two senses
nodes.rationale: There is no actual PENR Officer; the standing OIC has held the post for years and his title is what prints. Temporary cover while he is away lasts days and never reaches the system, being handwritten if written at all. Nothing to build for either sense.

nodes.label: Per procurationem signing
nodes.source_location: Vocabulary / Signing on behalf, as practised
nodes.rationale: Somebody signing on another's behalf with their authority, appearing as initials or a handwritten name and title in free space near the block. Observed four times on the CDS copies. Invisible to the system, because it happens with a pen after printing.

nodes.label: One person may fill two blocks of the same document
nodes.rationale: Allowed with no warning. A GSU staff member requesting fuel for a GSU vehicle qualifies for both Requested by and Approved by. The user watched an office head approve their own leave application when the usual approver was away, which is a stronger argument than a written rule. Nothing about a person makes them ineligible; the document decides.

nodes.label: Choosing the wrong person is not the system's problem
nodes.source_location: Choosing the wrong person is not the system's problem
nodes.rationale: The system stops only what is impossible, such as naming somebody who no longer works at the agency. If the wrong GSU staff member is named, GSU refuses to sign and the document is reprinted; deciding who ought to sign is the office's job and already works socially.
